claim: BOX-FDDP supports warm-started, single-iteration feasibility-driven constrained policy updates and Riccati feedback for empirical real-time MPC. It does not establish that every intermediate iterate is feasible or specify an interruption-safe deadline rule returning a previously certified feasible incumbent. It therefore supports fast feasibility restoration and RTI-like continuation, not deadline-total feasible-incumbent return.
epistemic_status: Solver formulation, implementation, and timing are author-reported; the absence of interruption-safe totality and per-iterate feasibility is an explicitly bounded reader inference.
problem_and_setting: Full-body hybrid legged-robot MPC must solve a nonlinear OCP with contact switching, dynamics equalities, torque/control limits, and friction/wrench-cone conditions within millisecond-scale control cycles. ANYmal experiments use predefined contact sequences and timings supplied by a planner.
method_or_mechanism: BOX-FDDP uses lifted multiple shooting and a feasibility-driven rollout that contracts dynamic defects. A bound-constrained QP computes feed-forward controls, feedback gains are obtained on the free-control subspace, and a Goldstein condition accepts steps. Each MPC update performs one warm-started solver iteration, reusing states, controls, and regularization. Riccati gains render task-priority-dependent feedback, while explicit control bounds are handled through projection onto the free-control space.
content_summary: The paper combines full-body hybrid predictive control, explicit actuation bounds, feasibility-driven BOX-FDDP updates, and Riccati feedback. Memory is preallocated; MPC runs at 50–100 Hz, with onboard operation reported around 90 Hz, while a 400 Hz tracking controller executes the policy. The approach empirically handles agile motions, disturbances, payload mismatch, stairs, jumps, torque saturation, slippage, and contact-timing error. Because trajectories may begin infeasible and feasibility is restored iteratively, it does not prove feasibility of every intermediate iterate or safe output under arbitrary interruption.
synthesis_role: Positive mechanism evidence for warm-started one-iteration constrained policy updates and Riccati gain rendering; negative boundary evidence against interpreting fast convergence as interruption-safe, deadline-total feasible-incumbent return.
development_link: For RMC-JOINT-UPDATE-TIME-FEASIBILITY, adopt feasibility-driven warm-started joint policy/gain updates as a computational precedent, but add an explicit certified-feasible-incumbent retention and deadline-return relation. Additional machinery is required for continuous soft-contact uncertainty and hard contact-constraint guarantees.

evidence.finding: Each MPC update uses a feasibility-driven DDP-type solver that explicitly handles control constraints.
Dynamic gaps contract and iterations are driven toward feasibility, showing an iterative feasibility-restoration mechanism.
Each update performs one solver iteration and warm-starts states, controls, and regularization from the previous MPC solution.
MPC computes policies at 50–100 Hz while the tracking controller runs at 400 Hz; delay compensation assumes current torque persists for about 2.5 ms.
Riccati gains follow the optimal MPC policy and yield task-priority-dependent variable feedback, with control limits projected to the free-control subspace.

evidence.locator: Formulation and absence of an interruption contract
evidence.finding: Gap contraction and empirical timing do not prove every intermediate iterate feasible or guarantee return of a certified feasible incumbent under arbitrary interruption.

boundary_conditions: Contact sequence and timings are predefined by a planner.
Validation is on ANYmal under the reported rigid-body/contact model and control architecture.
Control bounds are explicit, but some friction and wrench-cone inequalities are quadratic penalties.
The method may start from dynamically infeasible trajectories and iteratively contracts defects.
Reported 50–100 Hz or approximately 90 Hz execution is empirical and platform-specific.
No result certifies a feasible output after arbitrary solver interruption.
The paper does not evaluate calibrated uncertainty or held-out soft-material, geometry, sliding, and contact-history generalization.
assumptions: A useful warm start from the preceding MPC solution is available.
The planned contact schedule is supplied and sufficiently accurate.
The rigid-body and contact model is adequate for prediction.
Current torque can be treated as applied during an approximately 2.5 ms delay.
A 400 Hz tracking controller can execute the local policy between MPC updates.
Penalty treatment of friction and wrench-cone violations is acceptable in the reported experiments.

reported: Experiments encounter model mismatch, disturbances, payload mismatch, slippage, torque limits, and contact-timing errors; results are empirical rather than universal guarantees.
inferred: Intermediate iterates need not be dynamically feasible.
A single warm-started iteration does not itself guarantee feasible output before every deadline.
No certified-feasible-incumbent retention and deadline-return rule is specified.
Penalized friction and wrench-cone inequalities are not proven hard-satisfied at every iterate.
The evidence cannot support calibrated contact uncertainty or held-out soft-contact generalization.

conflicts_with: Any claim that BOX-FDDP proves every intermediate iterate feasible.
Any claim that it establishes a hard worst-case computation deadline.
Any claim that it returns a certified feasible incumbent under arbitrary interruption.
Any claim that penalized friction and wrench constraints are hard-satisfied at every iterate.
verification_status: Verified by an independent paper_reader against Controller-supplied inline full-text content only; no external search or local-path access was performed by the reviewer. Model identifier: gpt-5.6-sol.
